atoms.text: The murdered cop rebuilt as a cyborg: a man is resurrected as corporate property, so resurrection is also enslavement.
Corporate ownership of the police: a city privatizes law enforcement, so justice becomes a service with a profit margin.
The cyborg's residual memories: fragments of the dead man's life surface through the programming, so identity is a ghost in the machine.
The malfunctioning rival robot: a competing law-enforcement machine kills a volunteer, so automation's failure is public and political.
The human inside the product: the story asks whether a person survives being turned into a brand, so personhood is tested against property.
The prime directive that blocks justice: a corporate directive prevents the cyborg from arresting his own creator, so law and justice diverge.
The partner who remembers: a human colleague recognizes the man inside the machine, so memory is sustained by relationship.
Dystopian Detroit: crime, decay, and privatization make the city a laboratory for corporate rule.
The torture and murder: the hero's death is graphically staged, so the audience's desire for revenge is engineered.
Reaganomics as horror: public services become profit centers, so the monster is the business model.
The data spike: the cyborg accesses corporate records, so the investigation becomes a fight over information.
The executive who builds the cyborg: a middle manager treats a human corpse as a product launch, so ambition is the film's quietest evil.
The final memory test: the cyborg must remember his own name to reclaim himself, so naming is the last act of personhood.
The media satire: news broadcasts and commercials frame violence as entertainment, so the world's tone is numb.
The revenge plot: the story follows a familiar revenge arc but keeps interrupting it with corporate satire, so genre pleasure and critique coexist.
The body as brand: the cyborg's armor is a logo, so identity is literally worn as corporate design.
